title: A credit-score change can help produce later default for borrowers already near trouble
source_unit: NBER Working Paper 35508; credit-inquiry counting rule, score changes, and two-year default outcomes
geography: United States; consumers around a fourteen-day credit-inquiry scoring cutoff

observations.period: Credit records and two-year outcomes; paper issued July 2026

score_change.value: an additional counted inquiry lowered credit scores by about five points without changing the rest of the credit report

clean_record_default.value: default did not respond among consumers with clean records

prior_derogatory_default.value: default rose by 3.2 percentage points over two years among consumers with prior derogatory marks

self_fulfilling_share.value: at least 13% of the score-default relationship for consumers with prior derogatories was self-fulfilling

observations.method: The authors use a rule that counts multiple credit inquiries within fourteen days as one and estimate a regression discontinuity around the cutoff, treating the resulting score movement as a change that does not add a new credit-report fact.
observations.uncertainty: The public abstract does not identify which lender changed an approval, rate, limit, or timing decision, nor does it follow rent, insurance, work, utilities, recovery, or later applications. The self-fulfilling share is specific to the study population and design; it is not a universal effect of every score movement.
observations.subgroup: Consumers near the fourteen-day inquiry-counting cutoff, separated by clean records versus prior derogatory marks; liquidity, alternative lenders, income, housing, and proximity to approval thresholds can differ within those groups.
observations.counterinterpretation: A lender may ignore a five-point movement, or another unmeasured decision may carry the effect. A higher default rate can reflect changed terms, reduced credit supply, borrower self-withdrawal, or another channel; the study establishes the score-to-default effect but not the exact contract path.

related_sources.claim: NBER DOI record for Working Paper 35508

boundary: This record adds a feedback finding: a financial signal can become part of the risk it predicts for a defined higher-risk group. It does not establish a particular lender action, monthly price, housing or job consequence, recovery path, or political response for any individual borrower.
